front.title: Post-Session Execution Assurance (PSEA): A Deployment Architecture for the PSEA Token Profile

abstract.t: This document is Informational and describes a concrete deployment architecture for the PSEA Token Profile . The architecture defines the four-tier P/S/E/A enforcement model (Passive, Silent, Explicit, Authoritative), the HTTP Verifier endpoints used to submit Evidence, the AttestationBlock wrapper for platform attestation tokens, the Verifier Acknowledgement (ACK) format, the error-code registry, and the operational trust-state model. All token-level definitions -- canonical encoding, proof claim sets, hash-chain model, action-payload binding, EAT profile declaration, security and privacy considerations, and algorithm agility -- are normatively defined in ; this document references those definitions and describes how they are operationalized in a conforming deployment.

section.name: Introduction
section.t: This document specifies Post-Session Execution Assurance (PSEA), a wire protocol for verifying human authority at the moment a sensitive action is executed. PSEA does not replace authentication; it requires cryptographic proof of authority at the moment of execution, independent of prior session state.

section.name: The Authority Gap
section.t: For decades, session-based security has operated on the assumption that a successful authentication event at login time represents the user's identity and authority for the duration of the session. In modern systems, where actions occur long after the initial authentication event and context drifts continuously, this assumption is no longer reasonable: a session authenticated by a legitimate user at 09:00 carries identical authority at 15:00, even if the device has been compromised, the user has stepped away, or an automated process has assumed control of the session. Authentication answers "Did this entity present valid credentials at some point in time?"; execution authority answers "Is an authorized human, present, verified, and operating from a trusted device, approving this specific action right now?". The gap between these two questions is where risk materializes, and it is the problem PSEA addresses.

Concretely: a banking session authenticated at 09:00 is still "valid" at 15:00 when a high-value fund transfer is submitted -- yet session validity says nothing about whether the legitimate account holder, present and aware, actually approved that transfer at that moment, as opposed to a hijacked session, malware acting autonomously, or an unattended unlocked device. The same gap recurs wherever a high-consequence action rides on a still-open session: dispensing a controlled drug, recording a safety-critical shift check-in, or escalating an administrator's privileges. Session-valid is not the same property as this specific human approved this specific action, right now. PSEA's purpose is to produce cryptographic Evidence of the latter at execution time, independent of session state.

section.name: Document Scope and Status
section.t: This document is Informational and is submitted through the Independent Submission Stream . It defines the PSEA wire protocol: canonical encoding, proof token formats, the four enforcement tiers, trust state systems, verifier endpoints, error response codes, and accompanying security considerations. The wire formats and rules described in this document are sufficient on their own to build a conforming implementation; a reference implementation exists informatively but is not a normative dependency.

section.name: Applicability
section.t: PSEA is applicable to any deployment that needs an after-the-fact cryptographic record showing that a human user was present at a specific device at a specific moment and approved a specific action. The wire protocol is domain-neutral; this document does not enumerate or endorse particular industries or regulatory regimes, and does not claim compliance with any external compliance framework. Deployers are responsible for any compliance mapping they choose to claim against their own regulatory environment.

section.name: Requirements Language
section.t: The key words "MUST", "MUST NOT", "REQUIRED", "SHALL", "SHALL NOT", "SHOULD", "SHOULD NOT", "RECOMMENDED", "NOT RECOMMENDED", "MAY", and "OPTIONAL" in this document are to be interpreted as described in BCP 14 when, and only when, they appear in all capitals, as shown here.

section.name: Terminology
section.t: This document uses the following terms with the meanings defined here. Cross-references to the Remote ATtestation procedureS (RATS) Architecture are provided where applicable; the RATS role mapping in is informative. The normative wire shape is defined in .

dl.dd: The trust-anchor authenticator that generates Evidence by signing a proof token with a hardware-protected, user-verification-gated key. Per RATS, the Attester is the producer of Evidence. In PSEA, the Attester is a computational authenticator — it MAY be a smartphone, a smartcard with PIN, a FIDO security key with user verification, an embedded secure element, or any equivalent authenticator holding such a key; a natural person is not an Attester.

The server-side component that appraises Evidence and produces Attestation Results. Per RATS, the Verifier consumes Evidence and applies Reference Values and Endorsements to produce an Attestation Result.

The application server that gates the action. The Relying Party consumes the Attestation Result and decides whether to permit the action. The Relying Party MAY be co-located with the Verifier or operated as a separate service.

The natural person whom the Attester's Evidence makes claims about. The Subject is not itself an Attester. Presence and intent of the Subject at the moment of action are the central properties PSEA Evidence asserts.
The signed proof token an Attester produces. PSEA defines four Evidence types: ApprovalToken (Tiers E and A), PToken (Tier P), and SessionSummary (Tier S). See .
The integrity-protected artifact the Verifier produces and returns to the Relying Party, conveying the Verifier's appraisal of submitted Evidence.
A trust anchor a Verifier uses to appraise Evidence (for example, a platform attestation root such as the Android Key Attestation root or the Apple App Attest root).
Verifier-side appraisal policy inputs (expected attestation chain properties, device-state posture criteria, etc.) against which Evidence is appraised.

The specific operation the Subject approves (a wire transfer, a drug dispense, an administrative configuration change, an agent action). The canonical encoding of the action payload is hashed and the hash is included in the signed body of the Evidence (see ).

One of the four PSEA enforcement levels: Passive (P), Silent (S), Explicit (E), Authoritative (A). The tier of an action is endpoint-determined; the integrating Relying Party selects per action which tier applies (see ).

section.name: PSEA Architecture
section.t: This section borrows the vocabulary of Remote ATtestation procedureS (RATS) for conceptual alignment with the IETF security community. The terminology is used informatively only: PSEA is NOT a RATS profile and does not claim format-level RATS or CWT conformance. The Tier E / Tier A proof is an EAT profile (, Section 7): the token is an EAT-JSON claims-set carried inside a compact JWS (). It uses the registered EAT claims ueid, eat_nonce, submods, and eat_profile () for device-state conveyance, alongside the registered JWT claims () and the profile's psea_* extension claims (). The role mapping below is a descriptive analogy; the normative wire shape is defined in Sections 3 through 8 of this document.

tr.td: Generates Evidence bound to actions or session events using a hardware-backed key.
Consumes Attestation Results; permits or denies the action.
Signed proof token (ApprovalToken, PToken, SessionSummary; see )
The artifact the Attester produces and the Verifier appraises.
Verifier-signed appraisal returned to the Relying Party
Conveys the Verifier's appraisal to the Relying Party. MUST be cryptographically integrity-protected.
Authenticator attestation trust roots (for example an Android Key Attestation root, an Apple App Attest root, a FIDO authenticator vendor root, or a smartcard issuer root)
Trust anchors the Verifier uses to appraise an authenticator's Evidence.
Expected attestation chain properties and device-trust-state criteria
Not an Attester. The human is the subject the Attester's Evidence makes claims about.

section.name: The Passport Model in PSEA
section.t: PSEA's data flow resembles the passport model described in , Section 5.1: the Attester transmits Evidence to the Verifier; the Verifier appraises the Evidence and produces an Attestation Result that the Relying Party consumes. This resemblance is informative; the normative wire shape is in and in this document, not derived from RATS.

The Attester MAY relay the Attestation Result on behalf of the Relying Party (for example, an authenticator that delivers the Attestation Result to the application server it is acting on behalf of), but the appraisal authority remains with the Verifier. The background- check model defined in , Section 5.2 is not used by PSEA and SHOULD NOT be assumed by implementations.

section.name: Data Flow

figure.name: PSEA roles and data flow, in RATS terminology.
figure.artwork:
+-----------------+ (1) Evidence +-----------------+ | Trust-anchor | --------------------------> | Verifier | | device | (signed proof token) | | | (Attester) | +-----------------+ +-----------------+ | ^ | | user-verification event | (2) Attestation | (out of scope; see Section 2.6.2) | Result | v +-----------------+ +-----------------+ | Human user | | Relying Party | | (Subject of | | (action gate) | | Evidence) | +-----------------+ +-----------------+
Auxiliary inputs to the Verifier (per RATS): - Endorsements: platform attestation trust roots - Reference Values: expected attestation chain properties, expected device-trust-state criteria

section.t: Arrow (1) carries Evidence: the signed proof token defined in . Arrow (2) carries the Attestation Result, integrity-protected by the Verifier. The user-verification event at the device is the subject of ; the mechanism is out of scope of this specification.

section.name: Co-location of Verifier and Relying Party
section.t: A PSEA implementation MAY co-locate the Verifier and the Relying Party in a single deployment (the Relying Party's backend both appraises Evidence and gates the action). It MAY also separate them (the Verifier is operated as an independent service whose Attestation Results are consumed by multiple Relying Parties).

The Verifier MUST produce Attestation Results that are cryptographically integrity- protected so that a non-co-located Relying Party can verify their authenticity independently. The wire format of the Attestation Result is defined in .

section.name: Subject Distinction
section.t: The trust-anchor device is the sole Attester in a PSEA deployment. Natural persons are not Attesters, in the sense of , Section 3.1: the Attester role is restricted to computational devices capable of generating Evidence. The human is the subject of the Evidence the Attester produces. states the normative requirement that the Attester's Evidence include a cryptographic binding to a user-verification event at the moment (or, for Tier S, at the bootstrap) of the action being attested.

section.name: Architectural Principles
section.t: The following five principles are normative for PSEA-conformant deployments. They map directly to the wire-protocol requirements in , , and .

section.name: Execution-Time Proof
section.t: Evidence MUST be generated at the moment a sensitive action is approved, not in advance and not in arrears. Pre-generated or session-cached evidence does not satisfy this requirement (Tier S is the explicit exception, in which the bootstrap evidence is generated at session start and the session-cached maintenance evidence is permitted within bounded conditions; see ).

section.name: Human Presence Assurance
section.t: A PSEA-conformant tier that approves a specific action with execution-time human authorization (Tier E and Tier A; see ) MUST include, in the proof of approval, Evidence that a human user was actively present at the trust-anchor device at the moment of approval. The presence Evidence MUST be cryptographically bound to the signing operation that produced the approval.

A PSEA-conformant tier that produces background attestation without human action approval (Tier P; see ) does not require human-presence Evidence. The guarantee Tier P provides is defined in and does not include execution-time human authorization.

In all cases where presence Evidence is required, presence MUST be demonstrated, not assumed. Presence Evidence is distinct from identity recall, in which a system infers human presence from a prior authentication event such as login.

The trust-anchor device is the Attester and the human user is the subject of the Evidence the Attester produces. The human is not a separate Attester. PSEA proves that a human was present and approved this specific action; it does NOT identify which human — identity attribution is the deployment's responsibility and is out of scope of this specification. The mechanism by which the trust-anchor device verifies human presence is equally out of scope. Examples of valid mechanisms include (but are not limited to): a platform biometric subsystem (face or fingerprint match), a hardware token PIN entry, a magnetic-stripe card swipe combined with a PIN, a smartcard with PIN, a WebAuthn-style authenticator with user verification, or any other platform-provided user-verification primitive. The normative requirement is that some contemporaneous user-verification event gated the signing operation; PSEA is mechanism-agnostic about which.

section.name: Device-Bound Trust
section.t: Trust is anchored in the specific physical authenticator that performed the user-verification event. The Attester's signing key MUST be hardware-protected (for example, in a Trusted Execution Environment, a Secure Enclave, a StrongBox, a smartcard secure chip, a FIDO authenticator's secure element, or equivalent), MUST NOT be extractable from the authenticator, and MUST be invalidated by the platform on revocation events (factory reset, re-enrollment of the platform user-verification credential set if the implementation binds the key to that set, etc.). Cross-device transferable signing material does not satisfy this requirement.

section.name: Cryptographic Proof
section.t: Trust is established through cryptographic mechanisms, not inferred from session tokens, cookies, or bearer credentials. The Evidence MUST be independently verifiable and resistant to replay, forgery, and delegation.

All four PSEA tiers and the Verifier acknowledgement are carried as JWS Compact Serialization (): the Tier E / Tier A proof, the Tier P PToken, the Tier S SessionSummary, and the Tier E / Tier A acknowledgement are each a compact JWS whose signature covers the received BASE64URL(header) || "." || BASE64URL(payload) octets, so peer verification is over the bytes on the wire and does not depend on re-canonicalization of the claim set. Canonical encoding per -- a simplified subset of the JSON Canonicalization Scheme () -- remains load-bearing for exactly one place where a hash is taken over canonical JSON octets: the action-payload binding (the SHA-256 over the canonical actionPayload that the Verifier re-computes and compares against the signed psea_payload_hash claim; ). The simplification -- integer-only numeric serialization -- is documented in ; an implementation that requires full conformance produces output identical to for that action-payload hash.

section.name: Connectivity Independence
section.t: A PSEA-conformant tier MAY require Verifier reachability for action approval, or MAY operate with deferred Verifier interaction, depending on the tier's security model.

Tiers P, S, and E (see ) MUST be capable of generating Evidence offline; Verifier-side appraisal MAY be deferred. Tier A () requires synchronous Verifier authorization and MUST NOT proceed without Verifier reachability; the Attester MUST surface OFFLINE_AUTHORITATIVE_BLOCKED () when the Verifier is unreachable.

In all cases, Evidence MUST be generated at the moment of action approval, not in advance and not in arrears. Deferred verification MUST NOT permit admission of stale Evidence or Evidence whose cryptographic binding to the action being approved cannot be established.

section.name: What PSEA Is Not
section.t: Clarity about the boundaries of PSEA is essential to prevent conflation with existing security paradigms.

PSEA is not Multi-Factor Authentication. MFA strengthens the login boundary by requiring multiple credential types. It does not address authority at execution time. Once MFA is completed, the resulting session carries the same inherited trust as any other session.

PSEA is not Continuous Authentication. Continuous authentication monitors behavioral or other signals throughout a session to detect anomalies. It is a monitoring and risk-scoring mechanism. It does not require Evidence of authority at the moment of a specific action.

PSEA is not Session Hardening. Session hardening techniques such as those described in -- short timeouts, token rotation, binding to IP addresses -- reduce the window of exposure. They do not verify who is executing an action within that window.

PSEA is not Risk-Based Authentication. Risk-based systems evaluate contextual signals to adjust authentication requirements dynamically. They operate at or near the login boundary. They do not provide execution-time Evidence.

PSEA is not a rebranding of Zero Trust. Zero Trust architectures reduce implicit trust between system components and enforce verification at network and application boundaries. PSEA addresses a different problem: the absence of verified authority at the point of action execution, which persists even within Zero Trust environments.

section.name: Verifier Acknowledgement (JWS)
section.t: On a successful Tier E or Tier A appraisal, the Verifier returns a signed Attestation Result as a JWS Compact Serialization object () — the acknowledgement, or ACK. Its protected header carries alg = "ES256", a kid selecting the Verifier's published acknowledgement-signing key, and typ = "psea-ack+jwt". The SDK pins the Verifier acknowledgement-signing key at build time and rejects an ACK whose signature does not verify against it.

The signed ACK applies only to Tiers E and A. The Tier P (/trustAttest) and Tier S (/sessionBatch) responses are not signed: they are plain JSON. Tier P and Tier S are device-to-server verification paths in which the server is the verifier of the Attester's signed evidence, not a signer of evidence returned to the Attester; there is therefore no signed acknowledgement back to the device for these tiers. A Tier P or Tier S producer MUST NOT require a signed acknowledgement and MUST treat the HTTP status code plus the plain-JSON body (including any registered error code from ) as the authoritative outcome.
The ACK payload carries JWT registered claims plus PSEA-private acknowledgement claims:

dl.dd: JWT registered claims (): acknowledgement identifier, issued-at (epoch seconds), and expiry (epoch seconds).

The Verifier's decision for the appraised proof. MUST be the fixed string literal "ACK". A signed ACK always carries psea_verdict == "ACK"; rejection responses use a different non-ACK response path and do not carry this payload. Implementations MUST reject any ACK token whose psea_verdict is absent or is any value other than "ACK".
Identifier of the proof this ACK acknowledges.
Identifier of the enrollment the proof was verified against.
The accepted monotonic counter value.
The Verifier-computed chainEntry () for this proof. The SDK persists it as the next proof's psea_chain_prev.
Boolean result of the fail-closed action-binding check ().

The deployment policy evaluation result for this action. When present, its decision field MUST be one of exactly: "APPROVE", "STEP_UP", or "DENY". These are a closed value set; no other values are defined. The psea_policy_verdict object also carries a reasons array of {code, humanText} objects. The internal evaluator verb WEBHOOK_HANDOFF is always resolved to either APPROVE or DENY before signing when a step-up webhook is configured; STEP_UP passes through as-is. psea_policy_verdict is omitted entirely on reject responses (where no ACK is signed). Implementations MUST treat an unrecognized decision value as an error.
Acknowledgement format version.
Boolean. Indicates the Verifier produced this ACK on a degraded appraisal path (for example, a fail-open on an unreachable auxiliary input). Present in the reference implementation's signed ACK.
String or null. A short machine-readable reason accompanying degraded; null when not degraded.
String. A short reason label present on some reject ACKs to disambiguate the verdict.
Boolean. Present when the deployment consulted an external approval authority; conveys that authority's decision.

section.t: The fields marked implementation-private above are emitted by the reference implementation's signed ACK and are documented here for completeness; a Verifier MAY emit them and a consumer that does not recognize them MUST tolerate them.

section.name: AttestationBlock
section.t: The AttestationBlock conveys the authenticator-issued attestation token that the Verifier uses to appraise the Attester's hardware-protected key against the authenticator's Endorsement (for example an Android Key Attestation root, an Apple App Attest root, a FIDO authenticator vendor root, or a smartcard issuer root). The wire shape of the AttestationBlock is intentionally minimal:
Field semantics:

dl.dd: A short identifier naming the attestation provider. Initial registered values: PLAY_INTEGRITY, APP_ATTEST. Future values are added via the IANA-managed registry in .

The platform-issued attestation artifact. The encoding is platform-specific: PLAY_INTEGRITY tokens are JWS-encoded; APP_ATTEST tokens are CBOR-encoded. The Verifier MUST parse token according to provider; no PSEA-defined canonical encoding applies to the token field itself.

section.name: Verifier Appraisal
section.t: The Verifier appraises the AttestationBlock by:

ol.li: Looking up the platform Endorsement (root certificate, public key, or equivalent trust anchor) for the named provider.
Parsing the token per the provider-specific format and validating its chain or signature against the Endorsement.
Extracting per-provider properties (package name / bundle identifier, security level, attestation challenge value, etc.) and comparing them to the Verifier's Reference Values.

Returning a per-provider rejection code (INTEGRITY_VERIFICATION_FAILED, INTEGRITY_PROVIDER_UNSUPPORTED, INTEGRITY_PROVIDER_INSUFFICIENT, ATTESTATION_SECURITY_LEVEL_INSUFFICIENT; see ) on failure, or proceeding to subsequent appraisal steps on success.

section.t: The internal structure of the token, the chain validation rules for each provider, and the choice of Reference Values are out of scope of this document; they are defined by the platform vendor's attestation specification and by the deployment's policy respectively.

section.name: Enforcement Tiers
section.t: PSEA defines four enforcement tiers -- Passive (P), Silent (S), Explicit (E), Authoritative (A) -- each with distinct connectivity, presence, and verifier-interaction requirements. The integrating Relying Party selects the tier per action; the tier choice is not a global per-user property. A single deployment commonly mixes tiers (for example, Tier P background attestation on every action plus Tier A synchronous authorization on high-value transfers).

section.name: Tier Model: Primitives and Composition
section.t: Tiers P, E, and A are atomic primitives, each with a fully-defined wire shape and verifier contract. Tier S is a composition primitive defined in terms of a bootstrap sub-primitive (Tier E or Tier A) and a maintenance sub-primitive (Tier P-cached or Tier P-live); see .

tr.td: Optional (Verifier accepts when reachable; produced offline-capable)
At session bootstrap (via Tier E or Tier A)
No per-action proof; one SessionSummary per session

section.name: Common Preconditions
section.t: The following preconditions MUST hold for every tier:

ul.li: The Attester's enrollment is in the Verifier's ACTIVE state (see ).
The Attester's local trust state permits proof emission for the requested tier (see ).

section.name: Tier P -- Passive
section.t: Tier P produces background-attestation Evidence without human action approval. The Attester emits a PToken at scheduled intervals or in response to host-application triggers; the PToken is signed by a deployment-specific passive-tier key (distinct from the user-verification-gated trust-anchor key used for Tiers E and A) and conveys the Attester's current trust posture without committing to a specific action.

The PToken is a JWS Compact Serialization object () whose protected header is {"alg":"ES256","kid":<passiveKeyHash>,"typ":"psea-ptoken+jwt"}, where kid is the standard-base64 SHA-256 of the passive-tier signing-key SPKI. Its claim set is: the JWT registered claims jti, aud, iss, iat, and exp; the EAT claim ueid; and the PSEA-private claims psea_counter, psea_tier, and psea_user_hash (omitted when blank), plus the OPTIONAL psea_action_context_hash, psea_device_state_hash, and eat_nonce. The cross-replay binding () is carried as psea_tier == "P" (authority level), aud == "trustAttest" (endpoint), and iss (deployment / tenant identifier). The PToken carries no psea_payload_hash and no psea_chain_prev (Tier P does not bind to an action and is not part of the per-action hash chain), and carries no eat_profile and no psea_uv (Tier P is not the EAT-profile execution-authority proof and makes no user-presence claim). The Verifier verifies the JWS signature over the received header.payload octets against the enrolled passive-tier key selected by kid.

The Verifier appraises PTokens via the /trustAttest endpoint ( and ) and returns one of the P-tier rejection codes (PASSIVE_KEY_NOT_ENROLLED, MALFORMED_PTOKEN, WRONG_TIER, PTOKEN_EXPIRED, ACTION_REQUEST_NOT_FOUND, USER_BINDING_MISMATCH, TENANT_BINDING_MISMATCH; see ) on failure, or signs an Attestation Result indicating acceptance on success.

Tier P does not bind to an action payload and does not satisfy the human-presence requirement of . The integrating Relying Party MUST NOT use Tier P alone to gate execution authority on a specific action; Tier P is intended for background risk-scoring, every-action silent attestation, and agent activity audit.

section.name: Tier E -- Explicit
section.t: Tier E approves a specific action with execution-time human-presence Evidence. The Attester produces an ApprovalToken (), gated by a contemporaneous user- verification event (), and posts it to /verify.

Tier E permits deferred Verifier interaction: the Attester's local trust state and the user- verification ceremony at the Attester are sufficient for the host application to proceed with the action; the Verifier appraises the proof asynchronously on the next available connection. On Verifier rejection (any of the wire codes in ), the Attester transitions its local state per .
The Verifier's action-binding obligation for Tier E is specified normatively in : the Verifier MUST recompute the payload hash and reject with ACTION_BINDING_INVALID on mismatch, fail-closed.

section.name: Tier A -- Authoritative
section.t: Tier A is identical to Tier E in signed-body shape and presence requirements, but with two additional constraints: (i) the Attester MUST NOT proceed offline (Verifier reachability is required at the moment of action approval; on unreachable Verifier the Attester surfaces OFFLINE_AUTHORITATIVE_BLOCKED -- see ), and (ii) the Verifier's authorization decision is synchronously delivered to the Attester before the host application proceeds with the action.

The Verifier's action-binding obligation for Tier A is identical to Tier E and is specified normatively in . Tier A's stronger contract over Tier E is in the connectivity and synchronous-decision dimensions, not in the action-binding dimension.

Tier A inherits Tier E's runtime integrity-evidence appraisal obligation in full: the Verifier MUST appraise the envelope's integrityEvidence AttestationBlock () against the deployment's Reference Values at every Tier A proof submission, applying the same per-provider rejection codes as Tier E. A Verifier that enforces attestation appraisal at Tier E but skips it at Tier A is non-conformant.

A Relying Party MAY supply an optional ContextLock primitive in the /authorize request envelope; when supplied, the Verifier MUST validate the ContextLock independently of the action-binding step. The ContextLock provides an additional binding (typically to a Relying-Party- held opaque context value); a future revision of this document MAY normatively specify the ContextLock wire shape and processing rules.

section.name: Semantics (Bootstrap x Maintenance)
section.t: Tier S is a composition primitive. A Tier S deployment is fully described by two choices on the Verifier-side configuration:

tr.td: The once-per-session ceremony performed at session establishment. Runs as Tier E (offline-capable, async proof) or Tier A (synchronous Verifier authorization).
The per-action validation performed silently inside an established session. Runs as Tier P-CACHED (local trust-state cache, zero added latency) or Tier P-LIVE (synchronous /trustAttest per action).

section.t: The connectivity requirements of Tier S inherit from the bootstrap and maintenance choices, NOT from a separate Tier S primitive. A producer SHOULD expose these two sub-primitives as independently-controlled configuration options.

section.name: Session Lifecycle
section.t: A Tier S session is a producer-side cache of human-presence authority. The session has a stable identifier (sessionId), bounded duration (ttl), bounded action count (maxActions), and an end reason recorded at flush time. Every action performed within the session is gated by the maintenance sub-primitive; no per-action proof is transmitted.
A session MUST end (and a SessionSummary MUST be generated and queued for batch sync) when any of the following triggers fires:

tr.td: Wall-clock time since session start exceeds the Verifier-supplied ttl.
The session has produced maxActions actions.
Wall-clock time since the most recent in-session action exceeds the Verifier-supplied idleTimeout.
A host-application-supplied event matching the Verifier's configured trigger list fires. The session summary MUST carry a psea_trigger_event_name claim.
The host application explicitly invokes the session-invalidate API.

section.name: SessionSummary Wire Shape (Normative)
section.t: Every Tier S session terminates by producing exactly one SessionSummary, carried as a JWS Compact Serialization object () signed by the device-anchored trust-anchor key (the same hardware-bound key K_d used for Tier E and Tier A per-action proofs), and transmitted inside a SessionBatch. The SessionSummary JWS protected header is {"alg":"ES256","kid":<deviceKeyHash>,"typ":"psea-session+jwt"}, where kid is the standard-base64 SHA-256 of the trust-anchor key SPKI (the same kid derivation as the Tier E / Tier A proof). The batch body is { "summaries": ["<compact JWS>", ...] } POSTed to /sessionBatch. The JWS signature covers the received header.payload octets directly; there is no separate detached signature field. The summary claim set is:
section.artwork: SessionSummary JWS payload (claim set) = JWT registered claims (RFC 7519) "jti" ":" string ; session id "aud" ":" %s"sessionBatch" "iss" ":" string ; tenant id "iat" ":" integer-epoch-seconds EAT claim (RFC 9711) "ueid" ":" string ; RAND-type UEID, ; base64url(0x01||sha256( ; deviceId)); same as E/A PSEA-private extension claims "psea_tier" ":" %s"S" "psea_user_hash" ":" string ; base64url no-pad; ALWAYS ; present; "" when no user id "psea_session_started_at" ":" integer-epoch-seconds "psea_session_ended_at" ":" integer-epoch-seconds "psea_end_reason" ":" %s"TtlExpired" / %s"MaxActionsReached" / %s"IdleTimeout" / %s"ManualInvalidate" / %s"TriggerEventFired" "psea_action_count" ":" non-negative-integer "psea_rolling_hash" ":" base64-sha256 ["psea_trigger_event_name" ":" string] ; IFF psea_end_reason == ; "TriggerEventFired"
section.t: Field semantics:

dl.dd: Session identifier (the JWT jti claim, ), unique per producer-side session, chosen by the producer.
The JWT audience claim (). For Tier S it MUST be the literal string "sessionBatch" — the endpoint binding of .
The JWT issuer claim (): the deployment / tenant identifier the Attester has locally available at sign time — the deployment binding of .
Issued-at, NumericDate in epoch SECONDS ().
The RAND-type EAT UEID (, Section 4.2.1): base64url(0x01 || SHA-256(deviceId)), base64url without padding — the same encoding and value as on the Tier E / Tier A proof ().
The authority-level binding of . For Tier S it MUST be the literal string "S".
base64url (no padding) of SHA-256 over the subject identifier; audit attribution only. ALWAYS present on the SessionSummary — the empty string when the session has no associated user identifier.
Wall-clock timestamps in epoch SECONDS. psea_session_ended_at - psea_session_started_at MUST be less than or equal to the Verifier-supplied ttl plus a small grace window (RECOMMENDED <= 30 seconds).
One of the five normative codes from : TtlExpired, MaxActionsReached, IdleTimeout, ManualInvalidate, TriggerEventFired.
Total number of in-session actions performed before end. MUST be a non-negative integer.

Standard base64 (RFC 4648, Section 4) with padding of the SHA-256 over a canonical concatenation of action identifier hashes. The canonical formula is: (1) collect the SHA-256 hash string for each in-session action, (2) sort those hash strings in ascending lexicographic order, (3) join with ":" as separator and append a trailing ":", (4) compute SHA-256 over the UTF-8 bytes of the joined string, (5) encode as standard base64 with padding. When the in-session action list is empty, psea_rolling_hash MUST be the empty string. The producer MUST use this formula deterministically; replay of the same session yields the same hash. Verifier non-verification (normative): the Verifier does not recompute or verify psea_rolling_hash. It is carried as a self-asserted audit digest, not a server-verified security binding. S-tier audit-trail integrity for the rolling hash is therefore self-asserted; the authoritative integrity boundary for Tier S is the SessionSummary JWS signature ().
REQUIRED iff psea_end_reason == "TriggerEventFired". MUST NOT be present for any other end reason.

section.t: The three cross-replay binding properties () are carried on the SessionSummary as the psea_tier (authority level), aud (endpoint), and iss (deployment) claims. The Verifier MUST reject the batch with TIER_MISMATCH, AUDIENCE_MISMATCH, or TENANT_BINDING_MISMATCH () respectively if any of the three fails its byte-equality check; comparisons MUST NOT normalize case or whitespace. All three are claims in the JWS payload and are therefore covered by the SessionSummary JWS signature. Note that all timestamp claims on the SessionSummary are epoch SECONDS.

Authenticity and integrity of each SessionSummary are established by the JWS signature over its received BASE64URL(header) || "." || BASE64URL(payload) octets — the same ES256 P1363 (R||S) signature form as the Tier E / Tier A proof. There is no separate sessionSignature field; the JWS compact-serialization signature segment carries the signature.

section.name: Verifier Signature Gate (Fail-Closed at the Batch Level)
section.t: On receipt of a SessionBatch that carries at least one SessionSummary, the Verifier MUST execute the following gate BEFORE any persistence, counter increment, or downstream policy evaluation:

ol.li: Resolve the active enrollment record from each SessionSummary JWS protected-header kid (the standard-base64 SHA-256 of the trust-anchor key SPKI). If no active record is found, reject with HTTP 404 ENROLLMENT_NOT_FOUND.
Extract the enrollment's stored public key in SPKI form.

li.t: For each SessionSummary compact JWS in summaries in order:

ol.li: If the entry is not a well-formed compact JWS (three base64url segments) or its signature segment is absent or empty, mark the batch as failed with reason MISSING_SIGNATURE and break.
Verify the JWS signature over the received BASE64URL(header) || "." || BASE64URL(payload) octets against the enrollment public key using ECDSA P-256 / SHA-256.
If verification fails, mark the batch as failed with reason SIGNATURE_VERIFICATION_FAILED and break.

If any summary failed the gate, reject the entire batch with HTTP 401 SESSION_SIGNATURE_INVALID. NO summary in the batch MAY be persisted; NO counter MAY be incremented; NO downstream policy or audit-log entry MAY be written (other than a per-batch failure audit record). This is an all-or-nothing gate by design.
Otherwise (every summary verified), proceed to persistence, counter increment, and policy evaluation.

section.name: Transport Endpoint
section.t: The canonical transport endpoint for Tier S is POST /sessionBatch. Producers MUST NOT route Tier S proofs through the Tier E endpoint (/verify) or the Tier A endpoint (/authorize). Verifiers MUST reject any request to /verify or /authorize whose payload identifies as Tier S with HTTP 400 STIER_NOT_ALLOWED (see ) before consuming any per-tier counter or replay-anchor.

section.name: Preconditions
section.t: Bootstrap MUST satisfy the preconditions of whichever bootstrap sub-primitive is configured (Tier E preconditions or Tier A preconditions). The session summary MUST be flushed via /sessionBatch before the session is considered fully settled; until the flush completes the producer SHOULD retain the summary in durable storage and retry per its sync policy.

section.name: Negotiation and Tier Mapping
section.t: The Relying Party communicates the required tier for a specific action via deployment-level policy bundled into the action request. A representative mapping uses a four-level risk classification:

tr.td: Background risk-scoring; agent activity audit; balance lookups; pre-flight checks.
Low-risk in-session confirmations; EHR record reads; intra-session reads.
Per-action explicit approvals; transfers below high-value thresholds; drug dispense in non-critical context.
Fund transfers; beneficiary-add; dangerous drug dispense; AI-agent privileged actions; critical-infrastructure admin changes; bulk data export.

section.t: A Verifier MUST reject any proof submitted to a non-Tier-S endpoint whose risk-level identifies it as a Tier S proof, before consuming any per-tier counter or replay anchor ().

section.name: Conformance Checklist
section.t: An Attester or Verifier claiming PSEA conformance MUST implement at least one of the four tiers end-to-end as defined in this section. A claim of multi-tier conformance MUST be qualified by listing the tiers supported. Reference appraisal pseudocode for each tier is provided in .

section.name: Trust State Systems
section.t: PSEA defines two concurrent state systems that together govern whether a given proof is accepted at the Verifier. The two systems are distinct in their owner, persistence, and cardinality, and they reconcile through the wire protocol rather than through a shared mutable representation.

ul.li: Attester local trust state (): private to the Attester, real-time, four-valued. Gates proof emission at the Attester before any wire interaction. Informative.
Verifier enrollment lifecycle (): authoritative server-side record, durable, three-valued. Gates proof acceptance at the Verifier. Normative.

section.t: A device can simultaneously hold different values in each of the two systems without that being an error condition -- the systems are reconciled at proof-submission time, not continuously.

Earlier revisions of this document defined a third system, a one-shot signed trustState commitment carried on every per-action proof body. That wire field has been removed: it was a single-value self-assertion by the Attester, and the authoritative trust gate is the Verifier's own enrollment-status / revocation check (), not a value the Attester asserts about itself. A conforming Tier E / Tier A proof carries no trustState claim.

section.name: Attester Local Trust State (Informative)
section.t: A conforming Attester SHOULD maintain a real-time internal trust-state representation that determines whether a proof may be emitted for a requested action. The internal representation is private to the Attester; nothing about its structure is observable on the wire and no Verifier depends on a specific structure. The four-state structure below is the reference-implementation structure; alternative implementations MAY use different representations (including a single-bit "ready-to-sign / not-ready-to-sign" representation) as long as they gate proof emission per .

section.name: States

dl.dd: Default operating state after enrollment. The Attester has no concerning local indicators. Proof emission is permitted for all action tiers per the policy defined by the Relying Party.

The Attester has detected one or more downgrading-class local indicators. The Attester restricts proof emission to lower-criticality actions (Tier P and Tier S maintenance, plus Tier E for non-CRITICAL actions). Higher-criticality actions require step-up authentication before transitioning back to FULL.

The Attester has detected one or more escalating-class local indicators. All proof emission is suspended pending step-up authentication or operator intervention. The Attester MUST NOT emit a signed proof body while in this state.

The Attester has detected one or more revoking-class local indicators OR has received a Verifier-side revocation indicator (HTTP 403 TRUST_REVOKED) and mirrored the revocation locally. All proof emission is permanently blocked. Recovery requires a full re-enrollment ceremony; recovery in place from REVOKED is forbidden.

section.t: The categorization of specific indicators into downgrading-, escalating-, or revoking-class is an implementation decision local to the Attester. The Verifier does NOT observe individual indicators; it observes only the presence or absence of a signed proof body (an Attester whose local state disallows emission simply does not sign). The signal-collection mechanism and the appraisal logic that converts raw indicators into a state transition are outside the scope of this document.

section.name: Transitions
section.artwork: FULL <-- downgrade --> REDUCED <-- escalate --> ESCALATED | | | | revoking-class | revoking-class | revoking-class | indicator | indicator | indicator +-------------------------+--------------------------+ | v +---------+ | REVOKED | (terminal) +---------+ | | full re-enrollment ceremony v FULL
section.t: Transitions between FULL, REDUCED, and ESCALATED are bidirectional and SHOULD be driven by the indicator appraisal pipeline. Transitions into REVOKED are terminal; the Attester MUST NOT transition directly from REVOKED to FULL except through a successful re-enrollment ceremony.

section.name: Action Gating per State
section.t: "Conditional" means the Attester MAY emit a Tier E proof in REDUCED state only when the requesting criticality is below CRITICAL per AND the Attester's local policy admits proof emission in this state. A conforming Attester MAY choose to be more restrictive than this table; it MUST NOT be more permissive.

section.name: Verifier Enrollment Lifecycle (Normative)
section.t: A Verifier MUST maintain, per Attester enrollment, a durable lifecycle state taking exactly one of three values: ACTIVE, SUSPENDED, or REVOKED.

dl.dd: Default state set when an enrollment is created by successful device-enrollment ceremony. The Verifier MUST process proof submissions from ACTIVE enrollments per the per-tier rules.

Operator-controlled temporary halt. The Verifier MUST reject proof submissions from SUSPENDED enrollments with an implementation-specific 403 code. Suspension is intended for operational scenarios (customer-side investigation, billing hold) and MAY be reversed by the operator without requiring re-enrollment.

Terminal state. The Verifier MUST reject every proof submission from REVOKED enrollments with response code TRUST_REVOKED () and MUST NOT process the submission further. Revocation is not reversible in place; recovery requires the Attester to perform a full re-enrollment ceremony, which creates a new enrollment record.

section.name: Transitions
section.t: Transitions ACTIVE <-> SUSPENDED MAY occur repeatedly. Transitions into REVOKED are terminal for the affected enrollment record; recovery produces a new enrollment record rather than reactivating the revoked one.

section.name: Proof Acceptance per Enrollment State
section.t: Each proof submission MUST be evaluated against the Verifier-side enrollment state in the following order:

ol.li: If no enrollment record matches the Attester identifier carried in the proof body, the Verifier MUST reject with ENROLLMENT_NOT_FOUND.
If the matched enrollment record's state is REVOKED, the Verifier MUST reject with TRUST_REVOKED. The Verifier MUST NOT proceed to signature, counter, payload, or policy evaluation.
If the matched enrollment record's state is SUSPENDED, the Verifier MUST reject with an implementation-specific code identifying the suspension. The Verifier MUST NOT proceed to further evaluation.
If the matched enrollment record's state is ACTIVE, the Verifier proceeds to the per-tier evaluation pipeline.

section.name: Absence of a Wire trustState Commitment
section.t: A PSEA proof body carries no self-asserted trustState field. Such a field would be a single-value self-assertion by the Attester — an Attester that should not emit a proof simply does not sign one (), so a signed proof body already implies the Attester considered itself trusted; the field would carry no information the signature does not already imply. The authoritative trust gate is the Verifier's own enrollment lifecycle (), not a value the Attester asserts about itself.
A conforming Tier E / Tier A proof MUST NOT carry a trustState claim, and a Verifier MUST NOT require one. The error-code registry () defines no trust-state rejection code.

section.name: Authority for Proof Acceptance
section.t: The Verifier enrollment lifecycle is authoritative for proof acceptance. The Verifier MUST treat its own record of the enrollment state as the source of truth. The Attester's local trust state is not directly observable by the Verifier and MUST NOT be relied upon by the Verifier as authoritative for any decision.

The Attester's local trust state is authoritative for the decision to emit a proof. The Attester MUST NOT defer proof-emission gating to the Verifier; round-tripping a proof for state validation creates a wire-detectable side channel that this document forbids.

section.name: Disagreement Cases

tr.td: Normal path. Verifier accepts subject to per-tier rules.
Verifier observes silence. No wire signal is required from the Attester.
Verifier rejects per step 3. Attester learns of the suspension via the wire response.
Verifier rejects with TRUST_REVOKED. Attester MUST treat receipt of TRUST_REVOKED as a revoking-class indicator and transition its own local state to REVOKED.

section.t: The REVOKED row is the canonical wire-driven Attester-to-Verifier reconciliation event: the Attester does not poll the Verifier for the enrollment state; instead, the Attester discovers a Verifier-side revocation only when its next proof submission is rejected with TRUST_REVOKED. This is by design -- it keeps the wire footprint minimal in the steady state while guaranteeing eventual reconciliation at the next proof opportunity.

section.name: Out of Scope
section.t: This document specifies state systems and state transitions but does not specify the signal-collection mechanisms or appraisal logic that drive transitions in the Attester local trust state. The categorization of specific local indicators into the downgrading-, escalating-, or revoking-classes referenced in is an implementation decision local to the Attester. The Verifier observes only the presence or absence of a signed proof body; it does not observe individual local indicators and does not need to.

Similarly, the operator-side decision pipeline that drives the Verifier enrollment lifecycle -- specifically, the criteria under which the operator transitions an enrollment from ACTIVE to SUSPENDED or REVOKED -- is a deployment-level concern outside the wire-protocol scope of this document.

section.name: Verifier HTTP Endpoints
section.t: This section specifies the HTTP-bound endpoints a Verifier exposes for receiving Evidence and enrolling Attesters. The endpoints are the wire-protocol surface; alternative non-HTTP transports MAY be defined by future documents.

tr.td: Issue a single-use Verifier-bound nonce for an action.
Enroll an Attester by submitting platform attestation Evidence.
Submit a Tier P PToken for background attestation.
Submit one or more Tier S SessionSummary objects at session end.
Submit a Tier E ApprovalToken for asynchronous verification.
Submit a Tier A ApprovalToken for synchronous authorization.

section.name: Common Request Headers
section.t: Every request to a Verifier endpoint MUST carry:

ul.li: X-API-Key: the deployment-issued API key authenticating the Relying Party (for operator-facing endpoints) or the Attester (for Attester-facing endpoints).
Content-Type: application/json for JSON-encoded bodies; application/jose+json for JWS-encoded bodies.
X-Request-Id: an opaque client-issued correlation identifier (RECOMMENDED).

section.name: POST /attest/nonce
section.t: Issues a single-use, time-bounded Verifier-supplied nonce for an action. The Attester MUST include the issued nonce in the signed body's eat_nonce field; the Verifier MUST reject any proof whose eat_nonce does not match or has expired (response codes NONCE_EXPIRED, NONCE_REQUIRED, NONCE_MISMATCH; see ). Nonces issued by this endpoint are SHORT-LIVED (RECOMMENDED TTL: 60-300 seconds).

section.name: POST /deviceEnroll
section.t: Creates an enrollment record for an Attester. The request body carries the Attester's hardware- bound public key (SPKI form), a platform attestation token tying the key to a hardware-backed key store, and the deployment-specific subject and tenant identifiers. The Verifier appraises the attestation token against the platform Endorsement (see ) and, on success, creates an enrollment record in state ACTIVE.

Enrollment-specific rejection codes: ENROLLMENT_NOT_ATTESTED, APP_PACKAGE_MISMATCH, ATTESTATION_SECURITY_LEVEL_INSUFFICIENT, INTEGRITY_VERIFICATION_FAILED, INTEGRITY_PROVIDER_UNSUPPORTED, INTEGRITY_PROVIDER_INSUFFICIENT ().

section.name: POST /verify
section.t: Receives a Tier E proof transport body (). The Verifier executes the appraisal pipeline: enrollment lookup by the protected-header kid, JWS signature verification (), ueid validation (), counter check (psea_counter), chain verification, action-binding fail-closed check (), user-verification check (psea_uv; ), integrity-evidence appraisal of the body's integrityEvidence AttestationBlock () against the deployment's Reference Values, posture appraisal, and policy evaluation. On success, the Verifier returns a signed Attestation Result as a JWS acknowledgement (). On failure, the Verifier returns a wire response code from .

section.name: POST /authorize
section.t: Receives a Tier A ApprovalToken. The Verifier executes the same appraisal pipeline as , plus synchronous policy evaluation (no async deferral), plus optional ContextLock validation when supplied by the Relying Party. The action-binding check is fail-closed ().

section.name: POST /trustInvalidate
section.t: Transitions an Attester's enrollment to REVOKED. The request body carries the enrollment identifier, the revocation reason category, and operator authentication. On successful revocation, the Verifier persists the revocation metadata (revokedAt, revokedBy, revokedSource, revokedReason) and all subsequent proof submissions from this enrollment will be rejected with TRUST_REVOKED per .

section.name: Reference Schema
section.t: Detailed JSON Schemas for the signed-body and envelope shapes are provided in Section 4 of this document. Operational artifacts such as OpenAPI contracts and machine-readable test vectors are normatively unnecessary for conformance; if available from an implementation, they are informative.

section.name: Error Codes
section.t: This section defines the codes a Verifier returns to an Attester across the four signing-tier endpoints (Tier P /trustAttest, Tier S /sessionBatch, Tier E /verify, Tier A /authorize) plus the one Attester-side surface code. The codes are partitioned into active codes (the Verifier emits these today) and reserved codes (defined for forward compatibility).

Implementations MUST NOT return a generic AUTH_FAILED or any undocumented code in place of the specific codes listed below. The code enumeration is IANA-managed (). Audit-side fraud-alert labels and ACK-payload field values that are NOT wire response codes are listed separately in .

tr.td: Per-deployment rate limit exceeded. The response includes Retry-After.
The Attester's enrollment is in the REVOKED state. The Attester MUST transition locally to REVOKED and stop issuing proofs.
The Verifier has no ACTIVE enrollment matching the supplied deviceIdHash / deviceKeyHash.
The enrollment record exists but has no recorded device attestation. Re-enrollment is required.
The enrollment is past its operational grace window ().
The signed body's signature does not verify against the Attester's enrolled public key.
The ueid claim is not a valid RAND-type UEID (, Section 4.2.1): the decoded byte string is missing the 0x01 RAND type tag or is not 33 bytes long. See .

The signed psea_counter is less than or equal to the Verifier's stored counter for the (Attester, risk-level) pair. Counters are tracked per risk level (five counters total: LOW, MEDIUM, HIGH, CRITICAL, PASSIVE) rather than a single global counter per Attester; see for the rationale.
The signed body lacks the psea_chain_prev claim (Tier E / Tier A require it; ).

The signed psea_chain_prev does not link to the Verifier's stored chain state (strict-equality mismatch; ). This code is also reused for the SUSPEND escalation outcome of chain gap-tolerance (): a gap-tolerant Verifier whose tenant policy sets onExceeded == "SUSPEND" returns HTTP 401 CHAIN_PREV_MISMATCH on ESCALATE. There is no dedicated SUSPEND wire code.
The Verifier-issued nonce embedded in the proof has expired.
The associated action request carried a server-issued eat_nonce, but the signed body does not carry eat_nonce.
The signed body's eat_nonce field does not match the Verifier-issued nonce for this action.
The "actionId" has already been finalized in the action ledger. Idempotent retries return the original outcome.

The action payload supplied with the proof does not match the binding carried in the signed execution-authority token (see ). The Verifier MUST NOT mint a signed acknowledgement when this code is returned.
The signed psea_caller_package does not match any application registered to the deployment.
The signed body lacks psea_caller_package. The claim is required at this revision.
The package identifier extracted from the device attestation chain does not match any application registered to the deployment.
Tier S (riskLevel = MEDIUM) requests must be batched via /sessionBatch; /verify is reserved for Tier E.

The signed authority-level binding psea_tier (carried on all four tiers) does not match the receiving endpoint's expected tier (/trustAttest expects "P"; /sessionBatch expects "S"; /verify expects "E"; /authorize expects "A"). See .
The signed endpoint binding aud (carried on all four tiers) does not match the receiving endpoint's logical name (e.g., signed aud="proofAuthorize" submitted to /verify). See .
The signed deployment binding iss (carried on all four tiers) does not match the tenant the Verifier resolves from the request's API key (cross-deployment replay). See .
The eat_profile claim is absent or does not match the PSEA EAT profile identifier (urn:ietf:params:psea:eat-profile:1). The Verifier MUST reject a Tier E / Tier A proof on this condition ().
The Tier E / Tier A proof lacks the required "psea_uv" claim, or carries "psea_uv.verified" != true. The Verifier MUST require a contemporaneous user-verification claim ().

The signed "psea_uv" claim contradicts the authenticator's attested UV-enforcement property (e.g., "verified" == true while the attested key is not user-auth-gated). Returned only where the attestation conveys a UV-enforcement property to cross-check against ().
The platform-attestation security level is below the deployment's policy floor.
The deployment is in ENFORCE mode for integrity evidence but the request did not carry an "integrityEvidence" block ().
The Verifier appraised the "integrityEvidence" token (for example Play Integrity, App Attest, or any other registered provider) and rejected it.
The Verifier could not run the platform-specific verification.
The "integrityEvidence.provider" value is outside the registered set ().
The provider is supported but does not meet the deployment's policy floor.
The JWS signature over the received header.payload octets does not verify against the enrolled device key. Emitted on the Tier E / Tier A proof path.
The Verifier rejected the Tier E proof because the Attester's reported state diverged from the Verifier's record beyond the tolerated drift.
The Attester has no passive-tier key enrolled. Re-enrollment with passive-key registration is required.
The submitted PToken is not parseable as a well-formed compact-JWS PToken ().
A token submitted to /trustAttest does not carry psea_tier == "P".
The PToken's exp claim is in the past.
The proof references a push-initiated action_request that does not exist.
The PToken's "userIdHash" does not match the enrollment-bound userIdHash.
A SessionSummary in the batch is missing required fields.
A SessionSummary in the batch lacks the required psea_rolling_hash claim ().
One or more SessionSummary entries in the batch carry an invalid or missing signature; the entire batch is rejected ().
The Attester refused to issue a Tier A proof because the Verifier was unreachable (). Not a Verifier response code.

Reserved for forward compatibility; not emitted by an implementation that supports only the MTI algorithm. A Verifier that supports algorithm negotiation () MUST return this code for unsupported algorithm values.

Reserved for forward compatibility; not emitted by an implementation that supports only the current "body.version". A Verifier that supports multiple versions () MUST return this code for unknown version values.

section.t: Total: 45 wire response codes. The compact-JWS single-payload format carries no envelope-versus-body duplication, so no token/body consistency codes are defined (); the authoritative trust gate is the Verifier's own enrollment-status / revocation check rather than any self-asserted wire trust-state field. USER_VERIFICATION_REQUIRED and UV_CROSS_CHECK_MISMATCH cover the Tier E / Tier A user-verification claim per ; TIER_MISMATCH and TENANT_BINDING_MISMATCH apply across all four signing-tier endpoints per ; two reserved-for-forward-compatibility entries are included. Deployment-level licensing and quota rejections (for example, an exhausted monthly action quota or a tiered-actions feature that is not enabled for the deployment) are implementation-specific and out of scope for this protocol; they are not assigned PSEA wire response codes.

section.name: Audit-Side Fraud-Alert Labels (Informative)
section.t: The following labels are written by the Verifier into the deployment's audit log when specific fraud-class conditions are detected. They are not wire response codes; the Attester does not receive them directly. They are documented here so that operators reading audit logs and external SIEM consumers can correlate audit entries with the corresponding wire responses in .

tr.td: The Verifier-computed SHA-256 of the canonical action payload does not match the signed "psea_payload_hash". Fail-closed per .

section.name: Summary of Requested Registries
section.t: This document requests IANA to establish one new registry:
The PSEA Attestation Source Registry, the media-type registration, and the urn:ietf:params:psea URN sub-namespace registration are requested by .

section.name: PSEA Error Code Registry
section.t: Registration policy: Specification Required .

Initial contents: the 45 codes listed in . Each registry entry consists of: Code (string), Endpoint scope, HTTP / body classification, Category, Semantics text. The codes are reproduced here for the IANA-managed registry:

ACTION_ALREADY_PROCESSED, ACTION_BINDING_INVALID, ACTION_REQUEST_NOT_FOUND, APP_PACKAGE_MISMATCH, ATTESTATION_SECURITY_LEVEL_INSUFFICIENT, AUDIENCE_MISMATCH, CALLER_BINDING_MISMATCH, CHAIN_PREV_MISMATCH, CHAIN_PREV_MISSING, COUNTER_REPLAY, EAT_PROFILE_MISMATCH, ENROLLMENT_NOT_ATTESTED, ENROLLMENT_NOT_FOUND, GRACE_WINDOW_EXPIRED, INTEGRITY_EVIDENCE_REQUIRED, INTEGRITY_PROVIDER_INSUFFICIENT, INTEGRITY_PROVIDER_UNSUPPORTED, INTEGRITY_VERIFICATION_FAILED, INTEGRITY_VERIFICATION_UNAVAILABLE, INVALID_SESSION, INVALID_SIGNATURE, MALFORMED_PTOKEN, MALFORMED_UEID, MISSING_CALLER_PACKAGE, MISSING_ROLLING_HASH, NONCE_EXPIRED, NONCE_MISMATCH, NONCE_REQUIRED, OFFLINE_AUTHORITATIVE_BLOCKED, PASSIVE_KEY_NOT_ENROLLED, PTOKEN_EXPIRED, RATE_LIMIT_EXCEEDED, SESSION_SIGNATURE_INVALID, SIGNATURE_VERIFICATION_FAILED, STATE_DRIFT_REJECTED, STIER_NOT_ALLOWED, TENANT_BINDING_MISMATCH, TIER_MISMATCH, TRUST_REVOKED, UNSUPPORTED_ALGORITHM (Reserved), UNSUPPORTED_VERSION (Reserved), USER_BINDING_MISMATCH, USER_VERIFICATION_REQUIRED, UV_CROSS_CHECK_MISMATCH, WRONG_TIER.
Total: 45 codes.
